narrative:
The model estimates a 45% chance that you will leave your current job. Because this probability is high enough to flag risk, the organization has decided to deny your promotion.

The decision was driven primarily by three key aspects of your profile. First, the fact that you have received other job opportunities while working here was the strongest factor pushing the prediction toward leaving. Having external options often signals that an employee is considering or being actively recruited elsewhere, which strongly influenced the model in your case.

Second, your six to ten years of experience in this organization worked in the opposite direction. Most employees the model expects to stay have shorter tenure (only 34.9% are in the 6–10 year range), so your length of service here actually pulled the prediction slightly toward staying. However, this positive effect was not strong enough to outweigh the other signals.

Third, your overall career experience of six to ten years also contributed toward predicting that you will leave. Employees the model sees as likely to stay are more often early in their careers (50.4% have only 1–5 years total experience), so your mid-level experience level added further weight toward departure.

Taken together, the combination of external opportunities and your experience level created enough concern about retention that the organization chose not to promote you at this time. You and your manager should discuss what would increase your sense of long-term commitment and whether those external opportunities can be matched internally.
